Grammar · Lesson 8

Quantifiers much, many, a lot of

Ask and answer about quantity in real life: How many people are coming?, We don’t have much coffee left, and There are a lot of chairs.

≈ 55–65 min much · many · a lot of a few · a little how much · how many 11 interactive tasks
NoticeCompare questions about people and questions about coffee.
DiscoverMatch much, many, and a lot of to the noun and the sentence.
BuildChoose, type, read, and build quantity sentences.
UseAsk and answer how much and how many about your life.

Quantifiers answer one everyday question: how much is there? English splits the answer by one thing: can you count the noun, or do you measure it?

Two-minute retrieval

Three quick checks from earlier lessons

Answer from memory, then check. Say each complete sentence aloud.

1We need tomatoes for the salad.  (some / any, from A1)
2 two banks on this street.  (there is / there are, from A1)
3She two sisters.  (have got, from A1)

Notice before the rule

A kitchen check before shopping

"How many eggs do we have? Not many. And how much milk is there? Not much. But we’ve got a lot of rice, and there are a lot of tomatoes."

  • Which word goes with eggs, a noun you can count one by one?
  • Which word goes with milk, a noun you measure?
  • Which phrase appears in the positive sentences, with both kinds of noun?

Discovery check: choose the pattern

Questions and negatives take much or many. Positive sentences take a lot of.

1How people are coming?  (question, countable)
2How coffee do we have?  (question, uncountable)
3We’ve got chairs.  (positive)
4There isn’t juice.  (negative, uncountable)
5Do we need more plates?  (question, countable)
6There’s food already.  (positive)

The foundation: count it or measure it

You met this split in the A1 lesson on some and any. Every quantifier choice in this lesson starts with the same question about the noun.

type of nounexamplesthe test
countablecup → cups, chair → chairs, person → peopleYou can say one cup, two cups, three cups.
uncountablecoffee, milk, time, money, work, trafficNo plural form. You measure it: some coffee, a cup of coffee.

The system: much, many, and a lot of

Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns, mainly in questions and negatives. Use a lot of with both, especially in positive sentences.

sentence typecountable (cups, people)uncountable (coffee, time)
questionHow many chairs do we need?How much coffee is left?
negativeWe don’t have many cups.There isn’t much milk.
positiveWe have a lot of chairs.We have a lot of food.

In everyday positive sentences, a lot of sounds more natural than much or many. Say I have a lot of work, not I have much work.

Get to the root: counting and measuring

Each word thinks about quantity in a different way. Many counts units: one chair, two chairs, three chairs. Much measures an amount: you do not count coffee or time piece by piece, you ask how big the amount is. A lot of does not care about the difference at all. It simply means “a large quantity,” and that is exactly why it works with both kinds of noun.

wordhow it thinksworks withexample
manycounts unitsplural countable nounsmany cups, many people
muchmeasures an amountuncountable nounsmuch time, much coffee
a lot ofjust says “a large quantity”botha lot of cups, a lot of coffee

Follow the noun, not the thing

How much money do you have? How many dollars do you have?

You can count dollars, but money itself is uncountable in English. The grammar follows the noun you choose, not the object in the world. This is why the first question a quantifier asks is always: what kind of noun comes next?

Drill 1: choose much, many, or a lot of

In this drill, use much or many in questions and negatives, and a lot of in positive sentences. Let the noun decide between much and many.

1How time do we have before the meeting?
2Do you know people in this neighborhood?
3She gets emails every day.
4We don’t have milk left.
5How chairs do we need for Friday?
6They do work in the summer.
7Is there traffic in the morning?
8He doesn’t take photos on vacation.

Asking about quantity: How much…? How many…?

These two question frames run half of daily life: shopping, cooking, planning, and travel. The answer is often short and drops the noun completely.

questionnatural short answers
How many people are coming?A lot. / Not many. / Just a few.
How much coffee do we have?A lot. / Not much. / Just a little.

Small amounts: a few and a little

For a small quantity, English keeps the same split. A few counts a small number; a little measures a small amount. Both mean “some, not zero.”

small amountuse withexample
a fewplural countable nounsa few cups, a few friends, a few minutes
a littleuncountable nounsa little milk, a little time, a little sugar

For excess, add too: too many emails with countable nouns, too much noise with uncountable nouns. Too means more than you want.

Drill 2: type much, many, a few, or a little

Type one of these four: much, many, a few, or a little. Check the noun first.

1How money do we need for the tickets?
2How people work in your office?
3I only need minutes to get ready.
4There’s milk in the fridge, enough for one coffee.
5We don’t have cups, so bring yours.
6I don’t have energy after work.

Read and choose

A message about the office party

"Hi team! The office party is on Friday. How many people are coming? I think about thirty. We’ve got a lot of chairs, but only a few cups, so please bring one. We don’t have much coffee left, and there isn’t much juice either. Elena is bringing a lot of snacks, and we just need a little sugar for the cake. See you Friday!"

Drill 3: read, then choose

1. How many people are coming to the party?

2. What does the office need more of?

3. Who is bringing a lot of snacks?

Drill 4: build the question

Build the question. Cups is countable, so count it.

Drill 5: build the negative

Build the sentence. Coffee is uncountable, and the sentence is negative.

Drill 6: count the people

Tap the word that is wrong.

Drill 7: measure the time

Tap the word that is wrong.

Drill 8: say it, then reveal

Read the cue, say the full sentence aloud, then reveal only after you answer.

1 We have a lot of cups. Make it negative.

We don’t have many cups.

2 There’s a lot of coffee. Ask a question with how.

How much coffee is there?

3 They have a lot of meetings. Ask a yes / no question.

Do they have many meetings?

4 I have a lot of free time. Make it negative.

I don’t have much free time.

5 We need some chairs. Ask about the number.

How many chairs do we need?

6 There are a few cookies left. Now say the same about the cake.

There’s a little cake left.

Use it in real life

Your week: Say five true sentences about quantity in your week. I have a lot of meetings. I don’t have much free time.
Ask the teacher: Ask three questions with How much or How many, then react to the answers. How much coffee do you drink? How many students do you have?
Your kitchen: Describe what is in your kitchen right now. There’s a lot of rice, but there isn’t much fruit. We’ve only got a few eggs.
Your city: Describe your city or neighborhood. There are a lot of cafés. There isn’t much green space.
Too honest: Say two true sentences with too much and too many. I drink too much coffee. I get too many emails.

Reflect

Say the system back

Complete this aloud: “In questions and negatives, I use ______ with uncountable nouns and ______ with countable nouns. In positive sentences, ______ sounds natural with both. For a small number I say ______, and for a small amount I say ______.”

Then ask one How much question and one How many question about your real life, and answer them.

Final quiz: quantifiers in real sentences

1. How ___ sugar do you take in your coffee?

2. How ___ languages do you speak?

3. We don’t have ___ time before the flight.

4. I bought ___ oranges at the market.

5. There are only ___ cups left.

6. Add just ___ salt to the soup.

7. I can’t sleep. I drink too ___ coffee.

8. Which sentence is correct?
